input:
Compressors are among the most widely used machines in process plants, and the temperature at which the gas leaves a compressor is a figure with far-reaching implications for downstream equipment, for safety, and for energy use. In the case considered here, a single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar, with the air entering the machine at an inlet temperature of 313 K. If the compression is modelled as isentropic, in other words as a process that is both perfectly adiabatic and perfectly reversible, and if a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 is adopted for air, the discharge temperature works out at 481 K.

It is important to appreciate the idealisations that sit behind this figure. The model assumes that no heat whatsoever is transferred between the gas and its surroundings during compression, that frictional effects are entirely absent, and that air behaves as an ideal gas whose heat-capacity ratio does not vary across the temperature range involved. Provided those assumptions hold, the discharge temperature is governed solely by the inlet temperature and by the pressure ratio, and matters such as the physical size of the machine, the speed at which it runs, and the detailed design of its valves have no bearing on the outcome.

In practice, however, the position is somewhat different, because the isentropic estimate deliberately leaves mechanical losses out of account. In a real, installed machine there is friction in the bearings and in the seals, and there are irreversibilities as the gas passes through the valves, all of which convert a portion of the shaft work into extra heat within the gas itself. It follows that the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine will be higher than 481 K, in many cases noticeably so, and the estimate should be regarded as an idealised benchmark: valuable as a reference point for preliminary design and for judging the condition of a machine, but not a prediction of the temperature that will actually be observed in service.
target:
A single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar. The air enters at 313 K, and the discharge temperature on the isentropic estimate is 481 K.

The estimate treats the compression as reversible and adiabatic. No heat crosses the casing during the compression, no friction acts on the gas, and air is treated as an ideal gas with a constant heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 over the whole temperature range. Under those assumptions, the discharge temperature is fixed by the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio. The size of the machine, its rotational speed, its valve geometry, and its clearance volume do not enter the calculation, because none of them alters the end state of an isentropic compression carried out between the same two pressures.

The figure is the discharge temperature of the idealised machine, and it is a lower bound on the temperature the installed machine will reach. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. In the installed machine, friction in the bearings and seals and the irreversibility of the flow through the valves convert part of the shaft work into heat in the gas, and the measured discharge temperature is higher than 481 K. A measured temperature above the estimate is the expected outcome of the comparison; the estimate and the measurement describe different machines, one idealised and one as built, and a difference between them is not, on its own, evidence of a fault in either.

The estimate is used where the idealised temperature is the quantity the decision needs: a first sizing of the discharge cooler, an early check of the discharge temperature against a limit set by a seal material or a lubricant, and a baseline against which the measured temperature is read when the condition of the machine is assessed. Where the decision turns on the temperature the machine actually reaches in service, the measured discharge temperature displaces the estimate, and the estimate retains only its baseline role.
